stories.headline: Cool prices and weak shopping make a September Fed hike look less likely
stories.dek: U.S. inflation cooled, shops sold less, and traders now give only about a one-in-three chance that the Federal Reserve will raise borrowing costs next month.
stories.caveman: The United States has a money boss called the Federal Reserve, or the Fed. Its job is to keep prices from rising too fast without killing jobs. Last week two price reports came in softer than feared. Consumer prices, called CPI, rose only a little. Producer prices, called PPI, did not rise at all that month. Then shops said July sales fell 0.6 percent. People bought less stuff. That combo made traders think maybe the Fed will not raise rates in September. Markets now put the chance of a hike next month around one third. The chance of a hike by December is still close to half, because yearly inflation is still above the Fed's 2 percent goal. The U.S. dollar slipped under a score of 100 against other money. This week watchers will read the minutes of the Fed's last meeting on Wednesday. Later this month, bosses of many central banks meet in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. Chair Kevin Warsh has not said what he will do.
stories.why_it_matters: If the Fed holds still, loans and mortgages do not get even more expensive. That can help house buyers and companies. But if oil from the Iran war pushes prices up again, the pause could be short. Weak shopping also means some workers and shops are already hurting.
stories.camps: Stock investors mostly want the Fed to wait, because cheaper borrowing props up share prices. Some economists say cheering for weak shopping is dangerous: if people stop buying for too long, jobs go. The White House wants lower living costs before November elections. Critics say the Fed should follow the data, not the campaign calendar. Hawks on the Fed board already voted to hike last time and may still want a later rise.
stories.image_alt: The Federal Reserve building in Washington, shown in a finance-news graphic with a line chart

terms.explain: The main bank of the United States. It does not serve regular customers. It sets the price of borrowing money.
The extra money you pay to borrow. If the Fed raises this, mortgages, car loans, and credit cards get more expensive.
A monthly basket of what households pay for food, rent, fuel, and more. If CPI rises fast, life feels more expensive.
What companies pay for goods before they sell them to you. If this jumps, store prices often follow.
A monthly count of how much people spend in stores and online. A drop often means households are nervous or poorer.
The written notes from the Fed's rate-setting meeting. Markets read them for clues about the next move. The July notes come out Wednesday 19 August.
A yearly meeting of central bankers in Wyoming. The Fed chair often gives a speech there that moves markets. This year it is 27 to 29 August.
The current head of the Federal Reserve. He has not clearly said whether rates will go up in September.
A score that shows whether the dollar is strong or weak against other currencies. It recently slipped below 100.
One-hundredth of 1 percent. A 25 basis point hike means rates rise by a quarter of a percent.

stories.headline: Oil jumped about 6 percent this week as Hormuz stayed almost shut
stories.dek: Brent crude finished Friday near $88.50 a barrel after more tanker trouble in the Strait of Hormuz, and President Trump told Americans to accept higher gasoline prices.
stories.caveman: A huge share of the world's oil used to squeeze through a narrow sea lane between Iran and Oman. That lane is the Strait of Hormuz. Think of it as a one-lane bridge that most of the neighborhood must cross to get fuel. Since the United States and Israel started a war with Iran in late February, that bridge has been almost closed. Last week oil still rose. Brent crude, a world oil price, settled around $88.52 a barrel on Friday, up about 6 percent for the week. Two more ships were attacked in the waterway. Iran said on Saturday that America must accept defeat and that Tehran, not Washington, will decide when ships can pass. President Donald Trump told a crowd that paying a little more at the pump is the cost of the war. U.S. gasoline has been running far above last year. Households from Taipei to Texas feel this as higher fuel, food shipping, and airfares.
stories.why_it_matters: Energy sits inside almost everything you buy. When oil stays high, inflation stays sticky, and central banks find it harder to cut or even hold rates. East Asia imports most of its fuel, so a long Hormuz squeeze hits factory costs and household bills.
stories.camps: Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent say higher U.S. gas prices are worth it to crush Iran's economy. Iran says the strait is Iranian and will stay that way. Oil-importing countries in Asia and Europe want the waterway reopened for trade. Climate and left-leaning critics say a fossil-fuel war is making living costs worse for ordinary people while energy firms profit.
stories.image_alt: Ships and haze in the Strait of Hormuz off Iran

terms.explain: A narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf. Before the war, about one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil went through it.
A standard type of oil used to set world prices. When people say oil is at $88, they often mean Brent.
The fuel most U.S. cars burn. Americans talk about the price per gallon the way others talk about the price of rice.
A giant ship built to carry oil. Hitting one can spill fuel and scare other ships away.
When a navy tries to stop ships from reaching a country's ports. The U.S. says it is blockading Iran. Iran says it can still choke Hormuz.
The U.S. official in charge of money and sanctions. He said Washington will hit Iran with measures never seen as soon as this week.

stories.headline: Japan's central bank looks ready to raise rates in September
stories.dek: Three people familiar with Bank of Japan thinking told Reuters an early hike is in sight, and markets now price about an 80 percent chance of a move on 17-18 September.
stories.caveman: Japan's money boss is the Bank of Japan, often called the BOJ. For years it kept rates very low to wake up a sleepy economy. In 2024 it began raising them. In June it took the policy rate to 1 percent, the highest in 31 years. Now three people who know the bank's thinking told Reuters a September hike is likely. They also said the bank may raise rates faster than twice a year after that. Why? Oil from the Middle East war is pushing prices. Global demand for computers that run AI is strong. And the yen, Japan's money, is still weak, which makes imported food and fuel cost more in Japanese shops. Markets put the chance of a September rise near 80 percent. Japan's five-year bond yield jumped. Governor Kazuo Ueda said he will weigh inflation risks at future meetings. A U.S.-Japan effort last month to support the yen did not fully fix the slide.
stories.why_it_matters: When Japan raises rates, global money can flow back into yen and out of other markets. That can shake stocks, bonds, and the dollar. For Japanese households, a stronger yen would make imports cheaper. For borrowers, higher rates mean costlier loans.
stories.camps: BOJ hawks say inflation risks from oil, AI demand, and a weak yen are too big to wait. Doves worry Japan's economy is still fragile and that hiking too fast could hurt wages and small firms. The U.S. Treasury has nudged Japan about the weak yen. Exporters like a cheap yen because it makes Japanese goods cheaper abroad.
stories.image_alt: The Bank of Japan headquarters in Tokyo with the Japanese flag in front

terms.explain: Japan's central bank. It sets the country's interest rates and tries to keep prices stable.
Japan's money. If it takes more yen to buy one U.S. dollar, the yen is weak. A weak yen makes foreign goods cost more in Japan.
The head of the Bank of Japan. He said the bank may speed up rate rises if money is too easy.
The main interest rate a central bank sets. Other loan rates in the country tend to follow it.
The return you get for lending money to a government. When investors expect rate hikes, yields often rise.
When a government buys or sells its own money to change its price. Japan and the U.S. did this together last month.

stories.headline: Washington preps never-seen money pressure on Iran
stories.dek: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said new measures could land as soon as this week. Options include hitting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, more bank penalties, and a Senate bill that would restore tariff powers.
stories.caveman: The U.S. already uses trade bans, a naval blockade, and frozen accounts to squeeze Iran. Treasury's listings office has named more than 1,000 people, ships, and planes since President Trump returned to office. It says it froze about $500 billion in Iran-linked crypto. Still, oil keeps leaking out. China buys more than 80 percent of the Iranian oil that still ships, often through small independent refineries nicknamed teapots. On Friday Trump vowed to hit Iran hard. Bessent said the next steps have never been seen. Experts told Reuters the menu includes extra penalties on Chinese teapot refiners and banks, more hits on shadow oil ships, possible aviation curbs, even talk of a land cutoff with Iran's neighbors. The Senate passed a Russia-and-Iran bill last week that would also give Trump new tariff powers. The House has not agreed. The U.S. Supreme Court already struck down one legal basis for such tariffs.
stories.why_it_matters: Tighter measures can raise oil prices again and spill into food and shipping costs worldwide. Hitting Chinese banks could also sour U.S.-China talks before a possible Trump-Xi meeting. A land cutoff would squeeze Iranian civilians' food and fuel first.
stories.camps: The White House says maximum pressure will force Tehran to reopen Hormuz and talk. Iran's leaders say they already won concessions and will not bow. Experts warn a whack-a-mole hunt rarely changes Tehran's behavior. Democrats and some Republicans in the House worry new tariff powers would hit U.S. consumers and allies. Rights groups note ordinary Iranians, not just the state, pay the price.
stories.image_alt: U.S. President Donald Trump at a dignified transfer of remains of U.S. service members killed in the Iran war

terms.explain: Rules that freeze money, block trade, or punish anyone who does business with a listed person or country.
Punishments aimed not at Iran itself but at foreign firms, banks, or ships that help Iran sell oil or move money.
Smaller Chinese oil plants. They buy a lot of discounted Iranian crude and have little exposure to U.S. banks, so old penalties often miss them.
Aging oil tankers that hide their location or change flags to move banned oil.
Taxes on goods from countries that still trade with Iran. Trump wants this power. The Supreme Court struck down one legal path for it.
The U.S. Treasury unit that writes and enforces the lists of banned people, ships, and firms.

stories.headline: Stripe is said to buy AI switchboard OpenRouter for more than $7 billion
stories.dek: Bloomberg reported a deal for the startup that lets developers pick among 400 AI models. Stripe did not confirm. The price would be about five times OpenRouter's May valuation.
stories.caveman: Stripe is a big U.S. company that helps websites take card payments. OpenRouter is a young firm that does something similar for AI: one door, many models. A developer can send a question to OpenRouter and choose which brain to use, a cheap one, a smart one, or a specialist, from a list of more than 400. The startup says it has about 8 million users. In May it raised $113 million and was valued around $1.3 billion. Backers include Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, and Google's Capital G. The Wall Street Journal said last month that Stripe was in talks. On Sunday, Bloomberg said the talks became a deal worth more than $7 billion. That is a huge jump in a few months. A Stripe spokesperson told TechCrunch the company does not comment on rumors. If the report is true, Stripe would own a tollbooth on how businesses rent other companies' AI.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever owns the switchboard can steer money, data, and defaults toward some models and away from others. A payments giant sitting on that tap would have rare power over how companies buy AI, and over whether users can easily switch.
stories.camps: Fans say one gateway stops lock-in and lets small firms shop for the best model. Critics say a $7 billion price looks bubbly, and that putting the tap inside Stripe could create a new kind of lock-in. Stripe has not confirmed. OpenRouter's CEO once called his company Stripe for AI, which now reads like a hint.
stories.image_alt: A hand holding a phone that shows the Stripe logo, with a blurred market board behind it
stories.image_credit: Photo: SOPA Images / Getty via TechCrunch

terms.explain: A U.S. firm that lets apps and websites take credit-card and bank payments. It is one of the most valuable private tech companies.
A startup that gives developers one login to hundreds of AI models so they can pick by price and task.
What investors say a company is worth. OpenRouter was valued at about $1.3 billion in May. The reported sale price is over $7 billion.
A later round of investment after a startup has already proven some demand. OpenRouter's Series B was $113 million.
When it is hard to leave a product because your tools, data, or billing are stuck there. OpenRouter's pitch was to prevent that for AI.
The boss of OpenRouter. He compared the company to Stripe because it is a single access point.

stories.headline: Zuckerberg says AI is for everyone. A lot of people are not buying it
stories.dek: Meta's CEO published a 6,500-word essay and released an open model called Glimmer. TechCrunch's weekend show asked why the messenger makes the promise land so badly.
stories.caveman: Mark Zuckerberg, the boss of Facebook's parent Meta, wrote a very long essay this week. He said the future is for everyone. He pictured a personal AI agent that knows your goals and lives on your devices. Meta also put out Glimmer, an open-weight model people can download, while keeping a stronger model called Muse Spark behind paid doors. On Sunday, TechCrunch hosts said many readers are not sold. They pointed to Meta's history: a social network sold as connection that became ads and rage. Glimmer, they noted, is not actually easy for a normal person to run. You need special hardware. Zuckerberg also argued the U.S. cannot slow down versus China. Critics hear: do not regulate us. The essay is abstract when it talks about creativity, and concrete in ways that feel like always-on coaches some people do not want.
stories.why_it_matters: Meta has spent huge sums on AI talent and chips. If the public does not trust the company, that money may buy models nobody wants to live with. The fight also shapes whether open AI is a public good or a marketing line.
stories.camps: Zuckerberg says open models empower individuals and that slowing down helps China. Skeptics say Meta already broke a similar promise on social media, and that Glimmer-plus-Muse-Spark still keeps the best tools in Meta's pocket. Safety-minded labs want more brakes. Open-source fans want the weights, the hardware, and the governance, not just the slogan.
stories.image_alt: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaking at an event

terms.explain: The U.S. company that owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Reality Labs. Mark Zuckerberg is the CEO.
Meta's new AI model that anyone can download and run on their own machines, if they have the right chips.
Meta's more powerful AI, kept behind the company's own systems so Meta can charge and control it.
A model whose inner numbers are published so others can run and study it. It is more open than a chatbot you can only rent.
Software that is supposed to act for you: draft messages, run your calendar, maybe shop, not just answer a question.
The founder and boss of Meta. He has a long record of grand promises about connecting people.

stories.headline: Anthropic's boss says the AI backlash is really a crisis of trust
stories.dek: Dario Amodei answered critics who say his safety warnings hurt the industry. He said people already suspect tech firms are cooking up some new way to screw them over.
stories.caveman: Dario Amodei runs Anthropic, the company behind the chatbot Claude. An investor named Gavin Baker said Amodei's dark talk about AI danger has fed a U.S. backlash, especially against data centers, and that Amodei should be a cheerleader instead. On Saturday Amodei posted a long reply. He said his writing is half risk, half hope. He wrote an essay called Machines of Loving Grace to show a better future. He agreed the public view of AI is sour. He did not agree that his warnings caused it. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust, he said. Ordinary people, he argued, do not trust companies, governments, or tech. The fairest knock on AI firms, he added, is that they have not yet delivered big public goods, curing cancer, not just promising it. On rules, he said Silicon Valley treats regulation as a plot to help giants. Many people outside that bubble think rules can constrain corporate power. Anthropic, he said, tries to write rules that slow frontier labs and help smaller rivals, because AI tends to pile power on whoever has the most chips.
stories.why_it_matters: If the public does not trust AI companies, cities will fight data centers, workers will hide their use of chatbots, and Congress will stay stuck. Amodei's frame, trust not messaging, puts the burden on results, not slogans.
stories.camps: Boosters say safety talk is a marketing own-goal and that China will win if the U.S. hesitates. Amodei says the honest criticism is broken promises, not tone. Worker and consumer advocates agree on the trust point: people have watched social media, privacy scandals, and layoffs. Open-weight fans say his rules still risk helping the biggest labs.
stories.image_alt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaking into a microphone
stories.image_credit: Photo: Samyukta Lakshmi / Bloomberg / Getty via TechCrunch

terms.explain: A U.S. AI company. It builds the Claude family of chatbots and has pushed for some safety rules.
The boss of Anthropic. He talks often about both the benefits and the dangers of powerful AI.
Anthropic's main AI assistant. People use it to write, code, and answer questions.
A giant building full of computers. AI models need many of them. Neighbors often fight the noise, water, and power use.
The most capable AI systems, and the companies that train them. They cost billions in chips and electricity.
An essay by Amodei about how AI could help science and health if it goes well.

stories.headline: Apple warned iPhone users in 110 countries they may be spyware targets
stories.dek: A new lock-screen threat notification tells a small set of people that mercenary spyware may be aimed at their phone. Apple says the alerts are high-confidence and rare.
stories.caveman: On Thursday Apple sent a fresh wave of warnings. If you get one, your lock screen may say Apple detected a mercenary spyware attack aimed at your iPhone. That is not a normal virus. Mercenary spyware is expensive software, often sold to governments, used to break into a specific person's phone. Apple told TechCrunch the new batch reached users in 110 countries. Since 2021 it has notified people in more than 150. The company now puts the alert on the lock screen, not only in email, so it is harder to miss. Apple will not name the attacker. It says naming them would help the spies adapt. It advises turning on Lockdown Mode, a strict setting that has not, Apple says, been beaten in the wild. Researcher John Scott-Railton of Citizen Lab called the new alerts a big improvement. He said such pings helped uncover a spyware scandal in Poland's politics. Most people will never see this message. If you do, take it seriously, and beware of fakes.
stories.why_it_matters: These tools are used against journalists, lawyers, and opposition figures, not random shoppers. A visible warning can start investigations. It also shows how far commercial spyware has spread, including into democracies.
stories.camps: Apple presents the alerts as a duty to a tiny set of targets. Digital-rights groups want more help and, when possible, more public naming so governments can be held to account. Some states call the reports overblown. Security researchers warn scammers will copy the lock-screen text, so users should check their Apple account for a real listing.
stories.image_alt: An iPhone lock screen showing an Apple threat notification about mercenary spyware

terms.explain: Hacking software sold to governments and other clients to break into a chosen person's phone. NSO Group's Pegasus is the best-known example.
A high-confidence Apple alert that you, personally, may have been targeted. It now appears on the iPhone lock screen as well as by email.
A strict Apple setting that turns off many features so spyware has fewer doors. Apple says it has not seen a successful hack of a device that had it on.
A University of Toronto research group that tracks spyware abuse. Scott-Railton is a senior researcher there.
A digital-rights group. Apple tells alerted users they can call its 24-hour helpline for hands-on help.
Saying who did the hack. Apple refuses to do this in these alerts, arguing spies would learn how they were caught.

stories.headline: The 60-day U.S.-Iran deal expires with no peace and no open strait
stories.dek: A June memorandum was meant to end the war and reopen Hormuz. On Monday the clock runs out. Iran says the ceasefire never really started. Trump says there is nobody to negotiate with.
stories.caveman: On 17 June, President Trump and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a 14-point memo in Islamabad. It was supposed to stop the fighting, lift the U.S. naval blockade within 30 days, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. A final deal was due in 60 days. That deadline is Monday. Almost none of it happened. Trump called the deal over in July. The U.S. kept striking. Iran kept the strait tight. On Saturday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran has not decided to restart talks. Iran's version is that Washington never kept its promises on sanctions, frozen funds, the blockade, and Lebanon, so there was no 60-day ceasefire to extend. Trump told a New York crowd there is nobody to negotiate with, and that he may declare Hormuz U.S. territory after defeating Iran. Legal experts say a president cannot annex a strait like that. Mediators in Qatar, Pakistan, and Oman are still passing messages. The war is nearly six months old. Trump once said it would last four or five weeks.
stories.why_it_matters: As long as Hormuz is a battlefield, oil, food, and shipping stay expensive. The stalemate also bleeds into U.S. midterms: Democrats are already running on high prices and an unpopular war.
stories.camps: Trump's team still talks of total control and more pressure. Iran's new security chief, former IRGC head Mohsen Rezaei, signals a harder line. Iranian officials call the memo a victory on paper. U.S. polls show the war is unpopular. Analysts say a real deal may wait until after November, when the vote shock is smaller.
stories.image_alt: An anti-U.S. billboard in central Tehran, 13 August 2026

terms.explain: A written political deal that is less than a full treaty. The June U.S.-Iran MoU was meant to pause the war for 60 days.
Iran's president. He signed the June memo with Trump after talks hosted by Pakistan.
Iran's top diplomat. On Saturday he said Iran has not decided to restart talks with the U.S.
A hard-line commander newly put in charge of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, a sign Tehran may bargain tougher.
U.S. elections in November 2026 for Congress. Control of the Senate is in play. High prices and the Iran war are campaign issues.
Iran's powerful military-political force. It is separate from the regular army and has a big role in the war and the economy.

stories.headline: Ukraine and Russia trade one of the year's biggest nights of air attacks
stories.dek: Kyiv sent hundreds of drones at Russia, killing at least seven people by Russian count. Russia hit Ukraine the same night, killing at least seven more and burning a Kyiv book market.
stories.caveman: Overnight Saturday into Sunday, Ukraine launched what Russian officials called their largest air attack of 2026. Moscow's regional governor said about 600 of some 822 drones were aimed at the capital area. A warehouse of Wildberries, a huge Russian online shop, caught fire. Ukraine's defense ministry said seven of ten of the biggest Wildberries logistics sites are now disabled, claiming the hubs move military kit. An 83-year-old man died near Moscow. Five people died in Rostov. Russia hit back. Ukrainian officials said at least seven people were killed and dozens hurt. In Kyiv, sirens sounded four times. A book market in the Pochayna district burned. A stallholder's widow told the BBC she recognized her husband's books on the ground. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia fired more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided bombs, and 62 missiles at 13 regions this week. Ukraine still needs U.S. Patriot interceptors. Trump has been reluctant to send more because American stocks were used in the Iran war.
stories.why_it_matters: The ground war is stuck. Both sides now try to wreck the other's factories, shops, and nerves from the air. Civilians die either way. A shortage of U.S. interceptors leaves Ukrainian cities more exposed.
stories.camps: Ukraine says deep strikes are the only way to answer Russia's bombing of cities. Russia calls the drones terrorism. Each side accuses the other of hitting civilians. In the U.S., helping Ukraine now competes with the Iran war for missiles. Human-rights monitors said July was Ukraine's deadliest civilian month since 2022.
stories.image_alt: A huge plume of smoke over a Wildberries warehouse near Moscow as a firefighting helicopter approaches

terms.explain: A flying robot, often cheap, used to hit targets far away. Both Russia and Ukraine now fire them in the hundreds.
A giant Russian online shop, sometimes called Russia's Amazon. Ukraine says its warehouses also move military supplies.
A U.S. system that shoots down incoming missiles. Ukraine depends on it. U.S. stocks are low after the Iran war.
Ukraine's president. He said 13 regions were attacked this week.
A bomb given fins and a kit so it can steer onto a target from far away. Russia uses many of them on Ukrainian towns.
The long strip of land where the two armies face each other. Gains there have been small, so both sides hit deep behind it.

stories.headline: Zambia's president leads a tense count after vote-counting was paused
stories.dek: Hakainde Hichilema had about 55 percent with nearly half of constituencies in. Observers said intimidation and a Friday halt over stolen ballots stained the copper-rich country's test of democracy.
stories.caveman: Zambia voted on Thursday for president, parliament, and local seats. It is Africa's second-biggest copper producer after Congo, so the result matters for mines and debt. On Friday the electoral commission stopped the count, citing attacks on staff and stolen ballot papers. It started again after saying the threat was contained. On Sunday, with 105 of 226 constituencies declared, President Hakainde Hichilema had 54.8 percent. Challenger Brian Mundubile had 43 percent. If no one gets 50 percent, there is a runoff within 37 days. Mundubile's camp said he was detained; police denied it. He has claimed his own tally shows he won and has alleged meddling at tally centers. International observers on Saturday said the vote was marred by reports of intimidation, abductions, and the pause in counting. The European Union mission said democratic space was already tight. Amnesty International had criticized rights curbs before the poll. Hichilema is trying to turn pandemic-era debt repair into a second term.
stories.why_it_matters: A disputed copper-state election can shake mines, regional trade, and the idea that southern Africa still has room for ballots instead of guns. A runoff, or street unrest, would follow if the lead does not hold or if losers reject the numbers.
stories.camps: The ruling party says the pause protected the count and that Hichilema's economic record deserves another term. The opposition says the halt, security forces, and missing ballots look like a fix. Observer missions told both sides to cool the language and take fights to court, not the street.
stories.image_alt: An Electoral Commission of Zambia official in an orange vest examines a long ballot paper

terms.explain: Zambia's current president. He is seeking a second term after a debt crisis and some economic repair.
The main opposition candidate. His camp alleged interference and, falsely according to police, that he was arrested.
A second election between the top two if nobody wins more than half the vote. Zambia would hold one within 37 days.
The official body that runs the vote. It paused counting on Friday, then restarted it.
A metal used in wires, chips, and the energy transition. Zambia's mines make the election a global commodity story too.
Teams from groups like the EU and SADC who watch a vote and report on fairness. They cannot change the result.

stories.headline: Israel prepares to push Gazans south as Israelis strike to stop the war
stories.dek: The army said tents would go back into Gaza on Sunday while a wider offensive is planned. Hostage families called a nationwide day of stoppage. Gaza's health ministry reported 11 more malnutrition deaths.
stories.caveman: On Saturday Israel said it is preparing to move Palestinians from combat zones toward southern Gaza. The military aid body COGAT said tent deliveries would resume Sunday. Defense Minister Israel Katz talked of a plan to defeat Hamas in packed places including Gaza City and central camps. Families of the remaining 50 hostages, about 20 thought still alive, asked Israelis to halt daily life on Sunday. They fear a new offensive kills captives, not Hamas. At a Tel Aviv rally, relatives of the Bibas family and of Nepalese student Bipin Joshi pleaded for a deal. In Gaza, an airstrike killed a baby girl and her parents in a tent in al-Muwasi, an area Israel had called safer. The territory's health ministry said 11 more people died of malnutrition in 24 hours, one a child, bringing war-related malnutrition deaths to 251. The U.N. says starvation is at its worst since the war began. The U.N. human rights office counted at least 1,760 people killed while seeking aid between late May and last Wednesday. The U.S. State Department on Saturday froze visitor visas for people from Gaza while it reviews a few medical-humanitarian visas. Gaza's health ministry, whose numbers the U.N. treats as the best available, puts the death toll at 61,897.
stories.why_it_matters: A forced march south, more bombardment, and a visa freeze all shrink the space in which two million people can live. Inside Israel, the hostage movement is the strongest domestic pressure on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
stories.camps: Netanyahu's government says only a wider offensive ends Hamas. Hostage families, some ex-security chiefs, and street protesters want a ceasefire-and-swap deal now. Hamas still holds captives from the 7 October 2023 attack that killed about 1,200 people in Israel. Aid groups say Israel's restrictions, plus chaos at militarized food sites, are starving civilians. Israel says it targets fighters and blames Hamas for embedding among civilians.
stories.image_alt: Protesters in Tel Aviv around a bonfire, holding hostage portraits and a Hebrew sign that reads Strike

terms.explain: The Israeli military unit that controls what aid and goods enter Gaza. It said tents would resume on Sunday.
People seized by Hamas and other groups on 7 October 2023. About 50 remain, and families say roughly 20 may still be alive.
A crowded coastal strip in southern Gaza that Israel has at times called a safer zone. A baby was killed there in a tent on Saturday.
When a body does not get enough food. Gaza's health ministry counted 251 malnutrition-related deaths in this war as of Saturday.
A U.S.-backed, Israeli-supported aid scheme. The U.N. says many people have been killed near its militarized sites.
Israel's long-serving prime minister. He faces protests at home and an international outcry over Gaza.
The Hamas-led attack on Israel that killed about 1,200 people and started the current war.

stories.headline: A TikTok romantasy is the best-selling book in America this week
stories.dek: Hannah Nicole Maehrer's Adversary to the Villain is No. 1 on the trade-paperback list and No. 1 in the country, her second book in a row to do that.
stories.caveman: Romantasy is romance plus fantasy. On TikTok, that mix still prints money. Hannah Nicole Maehrer's series follows Evie Sage, who has been an assistant, an apprentice, an accomplice, and now, in book four, an adversary to the villain. Publishers Weekly, in its 17 August issue, says Adversary to the Villain is No. 1 among trade paperbacks and the No. 1 book in the United States. The last book in the series did the same. The first two each debuted at No. 1 in paperback and No. 2 overall. Fans are already guessing a fifth title that also starts with A. The cover is a joke-shop of evil office supplies: a good inbox, an evil outbox, a frog in a crown holding a SLAY sign. Serious literary novels are not what most U.S. book-buyers are taking to the beach. Closed-circle thrillers and romantasy are. Riley Sager's The Unknown is No. 2 in hardcover fiction. Chris Bohjalian's The Amateur, a Westchester golf-course thriller, debuted at No. 9 after a Bookstagrammer with almost 450,000 followers made it his August pick.
stories.why_it_matters: Charts show what the country is actually reading, not only what prizes honor. A TikTok series outselling almost everything means publishers will keep betting on romantasy, and on influencers who can move paper.
stories.camps: Fans say the books are funny, cozy-wicked, and a relief. Some critics call the trend formula. Booksellers still need the units. Hollywood scouts watch the same lists; the Bookstagrammer who picked Bohjalian works in TV acquisitions.
stories.image_alt: Cover of Adversary to the Villain by Hannah Nicole Maehrer, with a dragon, a crowned frog, and joke evil-office props

terms.explain: A story that mixes a love plot with magic, villains, and made-up kingdoms. It is huge on TikTok.
A larger, nicer paperback sold in bookstores, not the small mass-market size you used to see in airports.
The book side of TikTok. A few videos can put a paperback at No. 1.
A U.S. novelist whose villain-workplace romantasy series now tops the country.
A bestselling thriller writer. His 10th novel, about disappearances on a New England island, is No. 2 in hardcover fiction.
Book people on Instagram. Jordan Moblo, who also works in TV, made Bohjalian's The Amateur his August club pick.

stories.headline: A Pulitzer finalist sells a memoir about dying before the work is finished
stories.dek: Random House bought North American rights to Incomplete Works by Sarah Chihaya, who is writing toward her own death after a rare neurodegenerative diagnosis. Fall 2027.
stories.caveman: Sarah Chihaya is a critic in Queens, New York. She has taught at Princeton and NYU. She was a Pulitzer Prize finalist. Publishers Weekly's deals column for the week of 17 August says Random House editor Caitlin McKenna took North American rights to Incomplete Works. Chihaya has a rare, fatal neurodegenerative disease. She has long studied good death scenes in novels. Now she is writing toward her own death: what books get right and wrong about dying, and what it means to leave a life, and a self, unfinished. The publisher plans a fall 2027 release. Her agents are Hafizah Geter and PJ Mark at Janklow and Nesbit. The same column is full of other bets on grief and afterlives: a debut about siblings talking across death, a dark romance about hiring a killer, a Filipino folkloric Frankenstein from a trans angle. U.S. publishing is still hungry for intimate nonfiction that stares at the end without turning it into a TED Talk.
stories.why_it_matters: A big house paying for a memoir that may not have a tidy ending is a bet that readers want honesty about illness, not only triumph stories. It also puts a working critic, not a celebrity, at the center of the list.
stories.camps: Admirers of Chihaya's criticism will follow her onto the page. Some readers find illness memoirs exploitative. Her own frame is literary: she is testing the stories culture already tells about a good death. Random House is betting the test will sell.
stories.image_alt: Author and critic Sarah Chihaya, photographed by Beowulf Sheehan

terms.explain: A U.S. critic and essayist. Random House will publish her memoir Incomplete Works in fall 2027.
A runner-up for one of the top U.S. journalism and book prizes. Chihaya reached that list as a critic.
An illness that slowly damages the brain or nerves and cannot, today, be reversed. Chihaya is writing after such a diagnosis.
The right to publish a book in the U.S. and Canada. Other countries can be sold separately.
A major U.S. literary agency. Chihaya's agents there sold the memoir.
A large U.S. publisher inside Penguin Random House. McKenna is the editor who bought the book.

stories.headline: Max Porter's next novel is a one-day screenplay about an aging actress
stories.dek: Riverhead won U.S. rights to Burn and Rave, written as an imagined script. It is due February 2027, with a stack of foreign deals already in.
stories.caveman: Max Porter is a British novelist with a U.S. following. His books Grief Is the Thing with Feathers and Lanny played with form: verse, chorus, animal voices. Publishers Weekly says Parisa Ebrahimi at Riverhead won U.S. rights to Burn and Rave. The novel is written as a screenplay that takes place across one day. An aging actress named Lynette wakes hungover in a hotel and sets out to face her ghosts and the world's present mess. Rights are also sold in Canada, the U.K., France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and more. February 2027 is the U.S. date. Porter's U.S. publisher is a prestige imprint at Penguin Random House, the same corporate family that just bought Chihaya's memoir. The week's deals show houses grabbing unusual shapes, screenplay-novels, afterlife siblings, folkloric Frankenstein, not only more romantasy. Whether readers will follow a script on the page is the bet.
stories.why_it_matters: Form experiments only work if a publisher will print them. A transatlantic pile of deals for a one-day screenplay suggests literary fiction still has a commercial path that is not a TikTok romantasy.
stories.camps: Porter's fans like the risk. Some readers bounce off novels that look like scripts. Foreign scouts clearly did not. Riverhead's buy keeps him in the U.S. literary mainstream rather than a tiny press.
stories.image_alt: Novelist Max Porter

terms.explain: A British novelist known for Grief Is the Thing with Feathers. His new book Burn and Rave is due in the U.S. in February 2027.
A literary imprint of Penguin Random House in the U.S. It bought Porter's new novel.
A novel written as an imagined screenplay about one day in the life of an aging actress named Lynette.
A book that uses the look of a film script, scene headings and dialogue, instead of normal chapters.
Permission to publish a book in other countries and languages. Porter's new novel already has many of these sales.
Novels sold on style and ideas more than on a genre label like thriller or romantasy.

stories.headline: A cartoon skeleton from Instagram is America's top nonfiction book
stories.dek: Christian Watson's How Lucky Am I, starring Mr. Skelly, sits at No. 1 on Publishers Weekly's hardcover nonfiction list after the Oregon illustrator's following passed six million.
stories.caveman: Mr. Skelly is a gentle cartoon skeleton. He sits on rusty trucks, drinks tea, and reminds you that you will die, kindly. His maker, Christian Watson, is an animator from Myrtle Creek, Oregon. He drew the first Skelly in Tasmania in 2023. The character now has more than six million Instagram followers. The book How Lucky Am I, from Clarkson Potter, is an illustrated volume of those scenes. Publishers Weekly puts it at No. 1 on the hardcover nonfiction list. It was already an instant No. 1 New York Times bestseller. PW's reviewer called some lines cloying and the ending a wistful sigh: Skelly lights a match, puts on a kettle, and wonders if death is like being a cared-for child again. In a week of war news, a memento mori with wildflowers is what a lot of U.S. buyers took to the till. Other nonfiction on the list is harder: Annie Jacobsen's Biological War, political books, even JD Vance. Skelly outsold them in hardcover this measurement week.
stories.why_it_matters: Charts are not only for novels. A social-media artist can still beat Washington memoirs on paper, which tells publishers that comfort, death, and pretty bones are a real market, not only outrage.
stories.camps: Readers say the book is tender. Some critics call it trad-hipster and thin. Booksellers will take the sales either way. Watson presents the work as a reminder that everyone is made of the same bones.
stories.image_alt: Cover of How Lucky Am I by Christian Watson, with Mr. Skelly the skeleton sitting on a rusted truck holding a mug
stories.image_credit: Cover: Clarkson Potter / Penguin Random House

terms.explain: A cartoon skeleton created by Christian Watson. He stars in the bestselling book How Lucky Am I.
An Oregon-born animator and designer. He runs a studio called 1924us and drew Mr. Skelly in 2023.
PW's ranking of serious-looking hardback books that are not novels: memoirs, history, illustrated gift books.
Art that reminds you death is coming. Skelly is a soft, modern version of that old idea.
A Penguin Random House imprint known for lifestyle and illustrated books. It published How Lucky Am I.
The cash-register data behind many U.S. bestseller lists. PW's charts use it.

stories.headline: U.N. says 650,000 refugees in South Sudan may lose food aid
stories.dek: WFP and UNHCR warned Friday that a funding gap could cut rations for people who fled into South Sudan, even as about 3,000 more arrive from Sudan each week.
stories.caveman: South Sudan is a young, poor country. It also hosts hundreds of thousands of people who ran from wars next door. On Friday the World Food Programme and the U.N. refugee agency said more than 650,000 of those refugees are at risk of losing help. Without immediate funding, assistance will be reduced, said WFP's Adham Effendi. That could mean less food and less nutrition support for children and mothers. Many children already arrive hungry. About 3,000 refugees and returnees still come from Sudan each week because that war has not stopped. WFP said it is already giving only half a full ration to the most vulnerable, because it must choose. It needs $37 million to fill the hole now and $258 million to keep going through the rest of 2026. Rich countries have cut aid budgets while they spend on their own wars and borders. The people in the camps did not start those fights.
stories.why_it_matters: When rations shrink, children die first. A cut here also pushes families back toward Sudan's front lines or onto riskier roads toward Uganda and beyond.
stories.camps: U.N. agencies are begging donors. Donor governments say they are overstretched. South Sudan's own politics and violence make operations harder. Aid workers argue half-rations are a slow disaster, not a savings plan.
stories.image_alt: Women and children walking toward white humanitarian tents on a dusty path in a refugee settlement

terms.explain: The U.N. agency that feeds people in crises. In South Sudan it is already handing out half-rations.
The U.N. body that is supposed to protect refugees. It joined WFP's warning about the 650,000.
A person who has fled their country because of war or persecution. South Sudan is hosting people who fled Sudan and other neighbors.
The measured amount of food aid a person is supposed to get. A half-ration means they get about half of what they need.
Someone who goes back to their country after fleeing. Some Sudanese are entering South Sudan as returnees, not only as refugees.
The difference between the money aid groups need and the money donors actually send.

stories.headline: Fighting in Sudan drives thousands more from their homes in days
stories.dek: IOM said 4,250 people fled three North Kordofan villages on 14-15 August. Other U.N. figures this month: 18,000 newly displaced in West Darfur, and a $3 billion appeal only 40 percent funded.
stories.caveman: Sudan's war began in April 2023. The army and the Rapid Support Forces, once partners, turned on each other. The U.N. says tens of thousands are dead, about 13 million people have been pushed from their homes, and more than 30 million need help. This weekend the numbers moved again. The International Organization for Migration said 4,250 people ran from the villages of Um Arda, Tamid, and Al-Khor Al-Abyad in North Kordofan on 14 and 15 August. A rights group said an RSF attack in Um Arda killed 14 civilians on Friday. Many fled toward Omdurman, near Khartoum. In West Darfur, IOM counted about 18,000 people displaced from more than 20 villages in a week, most into Chad. Three health clinics in Central Darfur closed for lack of money, cutting care for about 75,000 displaced people. The year's $3 billion U.N. appeal has only $1.2 billion. RSF drones still hit El Obeid, the North Kordofan capital, while aid groups try to truck in water.
stories.why_it_matters: Sudan is already one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters, and it is still getting worse. When clinics close, measles, childbirth, and hunger kill people the bombs missed.
stories.camps: Both the army and the RSF blame the other and block aid when it helps their rival. The U.N. envoy is talking to both. Donors have underfunded the appeal. Neighboring Chad is absorbing new arrivals it can barely feed.
stories.image_alt: A woman in a green floral headscarf holds a small child at a camp for displaced people in Sudan

terms.explain: A Sudanese paramilitary force fighting the national army. It grew out of the Janjaweed militias of the Darfur war.
Sudan's regular army. It and the RSF were supposed to merge. Instead they went to war in 2023.
A U.N. agency that tracks people on the move. Its matrix counted the new North Kordofan displacements.
Someone forced from home who has not crossed a border. Millions of Sudanese are IDPs. Others are refugees in Chad.
A yearly ask for donor money. Sudan's 2026 appeal is about $3 billion and is only around 40 percent funded.
A city in central Sudan under pressure from RSF drones. Aid groups are still trying to deliver water there.
The U.N. office that coordinates emergency aid and publishes the funding numbers.

stories.headline: Zimbabwe ferry death toll hits 84, including at least 18 children
stories.dek: Police recovered more bodies from Lake Kariba on Sunday after an overloaded government ferry, licensed for 90 people, capsized in wind on Tuesday. Searchers are still looking.
stories.caveman: Lake Kariba is a vast man-made lake on the Zambezi, shared by Zimbabwe and Zambia. For villages on the Zimbabwe shore, a government ferry is often the only practical way to town because roads are broken. On Tuesday that ferry, run by the Rural Infrastructure Development Agency, flipped in heavy wind. It was licensed for 90 passengers. Estimates of who was aboard run from about 150 to more than 160. Seventy-seven people were rescued. By Sunday police said the dead numbered at least 84. At least 18 were children. Sixteen of those child victims were 10 or younger. The youngest was 1. Names on coffins at a memorial included Enita Mazhomba and Susan Muntanga. Hundreds waited at Kariba hospital to identify relatives. President Emmerson Mnangagwa called the wreck tragic and said it showed serious deficiencies. It is believed to be Zimbabwe's deadliest ferry disaster. The wreck was towed to an island. Divers have not found more bodies under it yet. Fishermen still are.
stories.why_it_matters: This is what crumbling public transport looks like: an overloaded boat because the state did not keep the roads or the passenger limits. Poor rural families pay first.
stories.camps: The government promises a fix and a dignified burial. Families want the missing found and answers about why a 90-person boat carried so many, including unticketed small children. Safety campaigners say Kariba's ferries needed rules and upkeep years ago.
stories.image_alt: A long row of named wooden coffins under blue tents at a memorial for Lake Kariba ferry victims

terms.explain: The world's largest man-made lake by volume, on the Zimbabwe-Zambia border. The ferry sank in its waters.
A Zimbabwe government body. It operated the passenger ferry that capsized.
A boat carrying more people than it is licensed for. This one was rated for 90 and may have held 150 or more.
Zimbabwe's president. He called the disaster tragic and said serious deficiencies must be fixed.
The big river that was dammed in the 1950s and 1960s to make Lake Kariba.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola workers walk out after months with no pay
stories.dek: Community tracers and hospital staff in Ituri say they have gone unpaid since the outbreak was declared in May. A treatment center closed Thursday. Africa CDC told the government to pay.
stories.caveman: Eastern Congo is fighting the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record. It is the Bundibugyo strain. There is no approved vaccine or treatment yet. Confirmed cases have passed 4,000, with more than 1,800 deaths. The people who disinfect rooms, bury the dead, and knock on doors to find contacts are often unpaid. Wiza Bondele, 29, told AP he was promised $510 a month. He has been working without pay since mid-May. One morning his motorbike ran out of fuel. He walked 13 kilometers. His shoes fell apart. On Thursday, staff at the Nizi treatment center struck and the site closed for a time. Gedeon Banga Ngbape, who leads contact tracing in Nizi, said his team has not been paid in more than three months. The government says it is cleaning fake names off the payroll and switching from cash to mobile money. Africa CDC's Jean Kaseya said the money is there and paying workers is Kinshasa's job. Meanwhile armed groups threaten teams, and some communities say Ebola is a hoax. Crowds have burned treatment centers and snatched bodies. Without tracers, the virus outruns the response.
stories.why_it_matters: Ebola control is contact tracing plus trust. Unpaid workers cannot do either. A strike in a record outbreak is how a local crisis becomes a regional one.
stories.camps: Health workers say they will not die broke. Officials say they must stop ghost workers before paying. Africa CDC sides with the staff: pay now. Communities burned by past epidemics distrust both the state and the white trucks. MSF and others warn the outbreak is still spreading faster than the hunt.
stories.image_alt: A health worker in a white protective suit with orange taped seams and red gloves stands in a rural Congolese village

terms.explain: A deadly virus spread by body fluids. This outbreak is the Bundibugyo type, which has no licensed vaccine yet.
Finding everyone a sick person met, then watching them. If tracers stop, the chain of infection goes dark.
A conflict-hit province in eastern Congo. It has about 90 percent of this outbreak's cases. Bunia is the capital.
The African Union's public-health agency. Its head told Congo's government to pay the Ebola staff.
Fake names on a salary list. Congo says it is checking lists because some unrelated names were added.
A medical charity. It has said this outbreak is still spreading too fast for the response to catch.
A way to bury Ebola victims without families touching the body. The rule saves lives and often causes rage.

glossary.explain: The Hamas-led attack on Israel that killed about 1,200 people and started the current war.
Iran's top diplomat. On Saturday he said Iran has not decided to restart talks with the U.S.
A digital-rights group. Apple tells alerted users they can call its 24-hour helpline for hands-on help.
The African Union's public-health agency. Its head told Congo's government to pay the Ebola staff.
A crowded coastal strip in southern Gaza that Israel has at times called a safer zone. A baby was killed there in a tent on Saturday.
The boss of OpenRouter. He compared the company to Stripe because it is a single access point.
A U.S. AI company. It builds the Claude family of chatbots and has pushed for some safety rules.
Saying who did the hack. Apple refuses to do this in these alerts, arguing spies would learn how they were caught.
Japan's central bank. It sets the country's interest rates and tries to keep prices stable.
One-hundredth of 1 percent. A 25 basis point hike means rates rise by a quarter of a percent.
Israel's long-serving prime minister. He faces protests at home and an international outcry over Gaza.
The return you get for lending money to a government. When investors expect rate hikes, yields often rise.
Book people on Instagram. Jordan Moblo, who also works in TV, made Bohjalian's The Amateur his August club pick.
The book side of TikTok. A few videos can put a paperback at No. 1.
A standard type of oil used to set world prices. When people say oil is at $88, they often mean Brent.
The main opposition candidate. His camp alleged interference and, falsely according to police, that he was arrested.
A novel written as an imagined screenplay about one day in the life of an aging actress named Lynette.
An Oregon-born animator and designer. He runs a studio called 1924us and drew Mr. Skelly in 2023.
The cash-register data behind many U.S. bestseller lists. PW's charts use it.
A University of Toronto research group that tracks spyware abuse. Scott-Railton is a senior researcher there.
A Penguin Random House imprint known for lifestyle and illustrated books. It published How Lucky Am I.
Anthropic's main AI assistant. People use it to write, code, and answer questions.
The Israeli military unit that controls what aid and goods enter Gaza. It said tents would resume on Sunday.
Finding everyone a sick person met, then watching them. If tracers stop, the chain of infection goes dark.
A metal used in wires, chips, and the energy transition. Zambia's mines make the election a global commodity story too.
A monthly basket of what households pay for food, rent, fuel, and more. If CPI rises fast, life feels more expensive.
When a government buys or sells its own money to change its price. Japan and the U.S. did this together last month.
The boss of Anthropic. He talks often about both the benefits and the dangers of powerful AI.
A giant building full of computers. AI models need many of them. Neighbors often fight the noise, water, and power use.
A score that shows whether the dollar is strong or weak against other currencies. It recently slipped below 100.
A flying robot, often cheap, used to hit targets far away. Both Russia and Ukraine now fire them in the hundreds.
A deadly virus spread by body fluids. This outbreak is the Bundibugyo type, which has no licensed vaccine yet.
A city in central Sudan under pressure from RSF drones. Aid groups are still trying to deliver water there.
The official body that runs the vote. It paused counting on Friday, then restarted it.
Zimbabwe's president. He called the disaster tragic and said serious deficiencies must be fixed.
The main bank of the United States. It does not serve regular customers. It sets the price of borrowing money.
The written notes from the Fed's rate-setting meeting. Markets read them for clues about the next move. The July notes come out Wednesday 19 August.
Permission to publish a book in other countries and languages. Porter's new novel already has many of these sales.
The long strip of land where the two armies face each other. Gains there have been small, so both sides hit deep behind it.
The most capable AI systems, and the companies that train them. They cost billions in chips and electricity.
The difference between the money aid groups need and the money donors actually send.
The fuel most U.S. cars burn. Americans talk about the price per gallon the way others talk about the price of rice.
A U.S.-backed, Israeli-supported aid scheme. The U.N. says many people have been killed near its militarized sites.
Fake names on a salary list. Congo says it is checking lists because some unrelated names were added.
Meta's new AI model that anyone can download and run on their own machines, if they have the right chips.
A bomb given fins and a kit so it can steer onto a target from far away. Russia uses many of them on Ukrainian towns.
Zambia's current president. He is seeking a second term after a debt crisis and some economic repair.
A U.S. novelist whose villain-workplace romantasy series now tops the country.
PW's ranking of serious-looking hardback books that are not novels: memoirs, history, illustrated gift books.
People seized by Hamas and other groups on 7 October 2023. About 50 remain, and families say roughly 20 may still be alive.
A yearly ask for donor money. Sudan's 2026 appeal is about $3 billion and is only around 40 percent funded.
The extra money you pay to borrow. If the Fed raises this, mortgages, car loans, and credit cards get more expensive.
Someone forced from home who has not crossed a border. Millions of Sudanese are IDPs. Others are refugees in Chad.
A U.N. agency that tracks people on the move. Its matrix counted the new North Kordofan displacements.
Iran's powerful military-political force. It is separate from the regular army and has a big role in the war and the economy.
A conflict-hit province in eastern Congo. It has about 90 percent of this outbreak's cases. Bunia is the capital.
A yearly meeting of central bankers in Wyoming. The Fed chair often gives a speech there that moves markets. This year it is 27 to 29 August.
A major U.S. literary agency. Chihaya's agents there sold the memoir.
The head of the Bank of Japan. He said the bank may speed up rate rises if money is too easy.
The current head of the Federal Reserve. He has not clearly said whether rates will go up in September.
The world's largest man-made lake by volume, on the Zimbabwe-Zambia border. The ferry sank in its waters.
Novels sold on style and ideas more than on a genre label like thriller or romantasy.
When it is hard to leave a product because your tools, data, or billing are stuck there. OpenRouter's pitch was to prevent that for AI.
A strict Apple setting that turns off many features so spyware has fewer doors. Apple says it has not seen a successful hack of a device that had it on.
An essay by Amodei about how AI could help science and health if it goes well.
When a body does not get enough food. Gaza's health ministry counted 251 malnutrition-related deaths in this war as of Saturday.
The founder and boss of Meta. He has a long record of grand promises about connecting people.
Iran's president. He signed the June memo with Trump after talks hosted by Pakistan.
A British novelist known for Grief Is the Thing with Feathers. His new book Burn and Rave is due in the U.S. in February 2027.
Art that reminds you death is coming. Skelly is a soft, modern version of that old idea.
A written political deal that is less than a full treaty. The June U.S.-Iran MoU was meant to pause the war for 60 days.
Hacking software sold to governments and other clients to break into a chosen person's phone. NSO Group's Pegasus is the best-known example.
The U.S. company that owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Reality Labs. Mark Zuckerberg is the CEO.
U.S. elections in November 2026 for Congress. Control of the Senate is in play. High prices and the Iran war are campaign issues.
A hard-line commander newly put in charge of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, a sign Tehran may bargain tougher.
A cartoon skeleton created by Christian Watson. He stars in the bestselling book How Lucky Am I.
A medical charity. It has said this outbreak is still spreading too fast for the response to catch.
Meta's more powerful AI, kept behind the company's own systems so Meta can charge and control it.
When a navy tries to stop ships from reaching a country's ports. The U.S. says it is blockading Iran. Iran says it can still choke Hormuz.
An illness that slowly damages the brain or nerves and cannot, today, be reversed. Chihaya is writing after such a diagnosis.
The right to publish a book in the U.S. and Canada. Other countries can be sold separately.
Teams from groups like the EU and SADC who watch a vote and report on fairness. They cannot change the result.
The U.N. office that coordinates emergency aid and publishes the funding numbers.
The U.S. Treasury unit that writes and enforces the lists of banned people, ships, and firms.
A model whose inner numbers are published so others can run and study it. It is more open than a chatbot you can only rent.
A startup that gives developers one login to hundreds of AI models so they can pick by price and task.
A boat carrying more people than it is licensed for. This one was rated for 90 and may have held 150 or more.
A U.S. system that shoots down incoming missiles. Ukraine depends on it. U.S. stocks are low after the Iran war.
Software that is supposed to act for you: draft messages, run your calendar, maybe shop, not just answer a question.
The main interest rate a central bank sets. Other loan rates in the country tend to follow it.
What companies pay for goods before they sell them to you. If this jumps, store prices often follow.
A runner-up for one of the top U.S. journalism and book prizes. Chihaya reached that list as a critic.
A large U.S. publisher inside Penguin Random House. McKenna is the editor who bought the book.
A Sudanese paramilitary force fighting the national army. It grew out of the Janjaweed militias of the Darfur war.
The measured amount of food aid a person is supposed to get. A half-ration means they get about half of what they need.
A person who has fled their country because of war or persecution. South Sudan is hosting people who fled Sudan and other neighbors.
A monthly count of how much people spend in stores and online. A drop often means households are nervous or poorer.
Someone who goes back to their country after fleeing. Some Sudanese are entering South Sudan as returnees, not only as refugees.
A bestselling thriller writer. His 10th novel, about disappearances on a New England island, is No. 2 in hardcover fiction.
A literary imprint of Penguin Random House in the U.S. It bought Porter's new novel.
A story that mixes a love plot with magic, villains, and made-up kingdoms. It is huge on TikTok.
A second election between the top two if nobody wins more than half the vote. Zambia would hold one within 37 days.
A Zimbabwe government body. It operated the passenger ferry that capsized.
A way to bury Ebola victims without families touching the body. The rule saves lives and often causes rage.
Rules that freeze money, block trade, or punish anyone who does business with a listed person or country.
A U.S. critic and essayist. Random House will publish her memoir Incomplete Works in fall 2027.

A book that uses the look of a film script, scene headings and dialogue, instead of normal chapters.

A later round of investment after a startup has already proven some demand. OpenRouter's Series B was $113 million.
